n: Woe to the comfortable elites of Jerusalem and Samaria who feel secure and important. Complacency is a spiritual danger — a warning repeated in the Book of Mormon for our day.

f.g: Mockingly, “the first of the nations” — they thought of themselves as top-tier.

n: Look at other cities like Calneh, Hamath, and Gath. Are you better than they? Those cities had fallen or would fall — so could you.

f.g: A major Syrian city on the Orontes River.

n: They push thoughts of disaster far away, yet their violent ways bring it closer.

f.g: The day of disaster or judgment.

n: They lounge on ivory-inlaid beds, eating choice lambs and fattened calves. This was luxury most Israelites could never afford.
They make up idle songs to the harp, imagining themselves as musical as King David — but without his devotion.
They drink wine by the bowlful and use the finest perfumes, but they don’t grieve at all over the coming ruin of their nation.

f.g: The ruin of Israel (the house of Joseph).

n: So those who were “first” in luxury will be first into exile, and their partying will end.

f.g: Hebrew marzeaḥ — a feasting club or revelry.

n: God swears by Himself that He despises Israel’s pride and fortresses, and He will hand the city over to its enemies.

f.g: The pride of Israel — their arrogant confidence.

n: Even if ten men survive in a house, they will die. The destruction will be thorough.

f.g: A small remnant; even that remnant won’t survive.

n: A grim scene: a relative comes to carry out bodies for burial. A survivor is told, “Hush! Don’t mention the Lord’s name” — afraid of drawing more judgment.

f.g: Possibly one who burns spices for the dead, or who burns bodies during a plague.
Hebrew has — “Hush!” — a word that sounds like our “shh.”

n: At the Lord’s command, both large and small houses will be shattered. No social class is exempt.
Do horses gallop on cliffs? Does anyone plow rock with oxen? Of course not — yet Israel has done something just as absurd by turning justice into poison.
They boast about capturing Lo-debar and Karnaim by their own power. Amos puns: Lo-debar means “nothing,” and Karnaim means “horns” (strength).

f.g: Hebrew lo dabar — also the name of a town Israel captured.
Hebrew Qarnayim — another captured town; horns symbolize strength.

n: God will raise up a nation — Assyria — to oppress Israel from its northern border to its southern edge, the very territory Jeroboam II had won.

f.g: Probably a valley stream near the Dead Sea, Israel’s southern limit.
